as_told: Before the 1930s Santa Claus wore many colours, often green. Coca-Cola's Christmas advertising dressed him in red and white, the company's colours. The red suit stuck, so the modern Santa is a creation of a soft-drink campaign.
lesson: Advertising can create a cultural tradition that people later take to be old.
what_happened: Coca-Cola's Santa advertisements painted by Haddon Sundblom began in 1931, and Coca-Cola itself says that Santa appeared in a red coat before Sundblom painted him. Santa in a red suit is in print well before that: in Sarah Addington's children's book The Boy Who Lived in Pudding Lane (Atlantic Monthly Press, copyright 1922), the young Santa is "always dressed in a bright red suit" and Mrs. Claus makes him twelve red suits. Coca-Cola says its advertising showed Santa from 1931 to 1964 and helped shape his image, but it did not give him the red suit.
false_part: Coca-Cola did not give Santa his red suit; he was shown in red before Coca-Cola's Santa advertising began in 1931.

lesson_verdict.why: Half of the lesson has a documented case: Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer was written in 1939 by an advertising writer at Montgomery Ward as a Christmas promotion, given to customers as a booklet, and later became a song and many products. I found no source that shows people later took such a tradition to be old, and no study of the question.

source.quote: as a Christmas promotion for the company

search_steps: English Wikipedia and the sources it cites: not checked separately; the debunkers listed below and Coca-Cola's own page were used instead.
Google Books API: refused with HTTP 429 earlier in this batch and again on one retry for this story; not tried further.

Open Library full-text search for Coca-Cola, Santa, "red suit" and invented: 2,094 hits. The earliest that tells the story is Peter Corey, Coping with Christmas (Hippo, 1999), page 166. The book is lending-only (full text refused with HTTP 401), so its words come only from search snippets, saved as JSON.

Joined snippets from four phrase searches give Corey's text as: "Coke was originally packaged in green. When they decided to make it red, they re-launched it using Santa dressed in a red suit, and the red suit stuck. Talk about the power of ...". Other hits: Arda, The truth about Christmas (2003), and a 2006 book saying Coca-Cola "actually invented Santa Claus". A 1976 book, The Santa Claus Book (E. Willis Jones), has a chapter called "Birth of the Red Suit" in its contents, so it does not credit Coca-Cola with the suit; not read in full.

Open Library searches for "Santa Claus in his red" and "Coca-Cola colors": a 1985 trivia book credits Thomas Nast with the red-suited Santa; a 2000 trivia book links the red trimmings to Coca-Cola colours. Snippets only; not quoted.

Tried free newspaper archives for a pre-1931 text: Chronicling America and loc.gov (HTTP 403), Papers Past (bot block), HathiTrust full-text search (HTTP 403), Utah Digital Newspapers (HTTP 418), Penn State newspaper archive (connection reset). Project Gutenberg returned HTTP 503. None retried.

A web search led to an archive.org scan of Sarah Addington, The Boy Who Lived in Pudding Lane (copyright 1922). Its full text, saved, has Santa "always dressed in a bright red suit" and Mrs. Claus making him twelve red suits.

Coca-Cola Company history page (saved): Sundblom's Santa debuted in 1931 in The Saturday Evening Post; the page also says Santa appeared in a red coat before Sundblom painted him, and that a 1930 Coca-Cola ad by Fred Mizen showed a department-store Santa at the soda fountain of the Famous Barr department store in St. Louis. Coca-Cola Canada FAQ page saved but its text did not load in the download.

Leads not used as evidence: Snopes, The Ferret, VERIFY and other debunkers point to Puck covers, an 1868 Sugar Plums advertisement and White Rock advertisements of 1915 and 1923; these are pictures and I did not find their text.
Searched for a correction by Corey: none found.
Open Library edition records for Corey's book: one edition only, Scholastic (Hippo), 15 October 1999.

For the lesson: searched for a documented case of a tradition created by advertising. The Dartmouth College Library Bulletin of November 1989 (Wayback copy of 2020, saved) records that Robert L. May created Rudolph in 1939 as a Montgomery Ward Christmas promotion. A first download of that page from the live site gave only a 'content has moved' page and was deleted.
confidence_note: The earliest telling found comes only from Open Library search snippets of a 1999 humorous children's book, and much earlier tellings probably exist in newspapers I could not search. The 1922 book shows that a red suit for Santa was in print before 1931, but it is one children's book, not proof that red was the usual colour; I could not get text from the many pre-1931 pictures of a red-suited Santa that debunkers cite. The lesson verdict rests on one documented case, Rudolph, not on a study; it supports only the claim that advertising can create a tradition. Open Library lists only one edition of Corey's book (1999); I did not confirm that it was first published that year.
